blocks.text: Some banks are so large that over-exposure to risk can make them fail and hurt millions of people. If governments understand the risks that banks run, they can frame better rules that push banks towards prudent decisions. A bank’s skill at managing risk also shapes investor behaviour: even a bank that earns large revenues can see profits fall if loan losses are not controlled, and value investors prefer banks that earn profits without risking heavy losses.

blocks.title: Where banking risks come from
items: Expected or unexpected events in the economy or in the financial markets.
Staff oversight or mala fide (dishonest) intention, which erodes asset values and so reduces the bank’s intrinsic value.

blocks.title: Eight headline risks in order
blocks.phrase: Large Crocodiles Move Carefully, Only Chasing Real Snacks.
blocks.note: Residual, dilution, settlement and counterparty risks sit in the credit-risk family; interest-rate and exchange-rate risks sit with market risk.

blocks.title: Big idea
blocks.text: Every risk is defined as the possibility of an adverse effect on the bank’s financial result and capital. Only the cause changes: default, cash shortage, rate move, fraud, rule-breaking, lost trust and so on.
Banks cannot remove risk, so they build a system to spot, measure and control it. A sound risk management system has six parts.

blocks.title: Six parts of a risk management system
items: Risk management strategy and policies, with procedures to identify and measure risk (risk assessment and management).
An appropriate internal organisation, that is, the bank’s organisational structure.
An effective and efficient risk management process covering all risks the bank is, or may be, exposed to in its operations.
An adequate process of internal capital adequacy assessment.

blocks.title: Six pillars of risk management
blocks.phrase: Sam Offers Pizza, Cola, Ice-cream and Cake.

blocks.title: Managing a risk step by step
items: Spot where the bank is exposed
Assess the size of the possible loss

blocks.text: **Liquidity risk** is the risk of adverse effects on the bank’s financial result and capital because the bank cannot meet its due liabilities. It happens when current sources of funding are withdrawn and the bank cannot raise new funds.

blocks.title: Two faces of liquidity risk
rows: Funding liquidity risk
The bank cannot raise new funds when its existing sources of funding are withdrawn.
Market liquidity risk
The bank cannot easily convert property or assets into liquid assets because of market disruption.
Availability of cash risk
Rising NPAs make banks afraid to lend, so less money flows in the market and liquidity falls.

blocks.title: How rising NPAs squeeze liquidity
items: Risk of non-repayment of credit grows
Less money flows in the market
Genuine customers do not get loans

blocks.title: Funding versus market liquidity
blocks.phrase: FUNDING = Fresh money can’t be raised; MARKET = Meltdown makes assets hard to cash.
blocks.note: Liquidity risk is also a consequence of large credit loss and business loss on the bank’s investments.

blocks.text: **Credit risk** is the possibility of adverse effects on the bank’s financial result and capital because a debtor defaults on its obligations to the bank. Several related risks are defined around it.

blocks.title: Credit risk and related risks
rows: Credit risk
Debtor’s default in meeting its obligations to the bank
Residual risk
Credit risk mitigation techniques turn out less efficient than expected, or do not reduce risk enough
Dilution risk
Purchased receivables lose value because of cash or non-cash liabilities of the former creditor to the borrower
Settlement or delivery risk
Unsettled transactions, or the counterparty fails to deliver in free-delivery transactions on the due date
Counterparty credit risk
Counterparty fails to settle its liabilities in a transaction before the final settlement of cash flows

blocks.title: Credit’s four relatives
blocks.phrase: Real Dogs Sit Calmly: Residual, Dilution, Settlement, Counterparty.
letters: Residual risk: safeguards weaker than expected
Settlement risk: delivery or settlement fails
Counterparty credit risk: other side fails to settle

blocks.title: Residual versus dilution
blocks.text: Residual risk is about collateral or other mitigation tools working worse than hoped. Dilution risk is about purchased receivables becoming worth less because of the seller’s own liabilities to the borrower.

sections.title: Market, Interest Rate and Exchange Risk

blocks.title: Price-related risks
rows: Market risk
Covers foreign exchange risk, price risk on debt securities, price risk on equity securities and commodity risk.
Interest rate risk
Adverse effect on the bank’s financial result and capital, on banking book items, caused by changes in interest rates.
Foreign exchange risk
Adverse effect on financial result and capital because of changes in foreign exchange rates. Also called currency risk or exchange-rate risk.

blocks.title: Four parts of market risk
blocks.phrase: Four Elephants Drink Cola: Forex, Equity price, Debt price, Commodity.

blocks.title: Currency risk has a second name
blocks.text: Currency risk, the risk of loss from fluctuating foreign exchange rates, is also known as exchange-rate risk. It affects anyone with exposure to foreign currency or to investments traded in foreign currency.

blocks.title: Exposure-linked risks
rows: Concentration risk
Arises directly or indirectly from the bank’s exposure to the same or similar source of risk, or the same or similar type of risk.
Bank exposure risk
Risks of the bank’s exposure towards a single person or a group of related persons.
Bank’s investment risk
Risks of its investments in non-financial sector entities, fixed assets and investment property.
Country risk
Risk linked to the country of origin of the person to whom the bank is exposed: the bank cannot collect receivables because of political, economic or social conditions there.

blocks.title: Do not put all eggs in one basket
blocks.text: Concentration risk is the danger of too much exposure to one borrower, group, source or type of risk. Spreading exposure is the natural cure.

blocks.title: Remembering the exposure group
letters: Concentration risk: same or similar source or type
Exposure risk: single person or related group
Investment risk: non-financial entities, fixed assets
Country risk: political, economic, social conditions

blocks.text: **Operational risk** is the possible adverse effect on a bank’s financial result and capital caused by omissions (unintentional or intentional) in employees’ work, inadequate internal procedures, poor management of processes, information and other systems, and unforeseeable external events. Operational risk also includes legal risk.

blocks.title: Operational family
rows: Operational risk
Employee omissions, weak procedures, system failures or unforeseeable external events
Legal risk
Loss from penalties and sanctions after court disputes over breach of contractual and legal obligations, and sanctions imposed by a regulator
Compliance risk
Loss because operations do not comply with laws, regulations, standards, anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing procedures, and other rules

blocks.title: What compliance failure can lead to
Operational risk sources
blocks.phrase: PEOPLE, PROCESS, SYSTEMS, EVENTS: the four ways operations go wrong.
letters: Omissions in employees’ work, intentional or not
Poor management of information and other systems
blocks.note: Legal risk is counted inside operational risk.

blocks.title: Image and direction risks
rows: Reputational risk
Possibility of losses because of adverse effects on the bank’s market positioning.
Strategic risk
Adverse effect on financial result and capital due to lack of suitable policies and strategies, poor implementation, or failure to respond to changes in the bank’s operating environment.

blocks.text: Reputational risk can arise from negative public opinion after a big fraud or scam, and when the bank cannot control its operational risk. Such events lead to non-repayment of loans, large debt and rising NPAs, and create a negative image of the bank. The PNB and ICICI Bank cases are cited as examples.

blocks.title: How a scam turns into reputation loss
Reputation formula
blocks.phrase: Credit loss + Business loss = Reputation loss.
blocks.note: A scam does not just cost money; it costs customers’ trust, which hits business.

sections.title: Capital Adequacy, Stressed Assets and Recovery

blocks.title: Capital terms linked to risk
rows: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR)
A bank’s capital measured against its risk-weighted assets; it shows how much cushion the bank has against risk.
Tier-I capital
Core capital: paid-up capital, statutory reserves and capital reserves.
Tier-II capital
Supplementary capital, which includes subordinated debt.
Risk-weighted assets
Assets weighted for credit risk, market risk and operational risk.
Basel III norms
Capital norms that raise the level of capital banks must hold.

blocks.title: Tier-I versus Tier-II
blocks.phrase: Tier-I is PSC: Paid-up capital, Statutory reserves, Capital reserves. Debt is second-tier: subordinated debt sits in Tier-II.

blocks.title: Bad loans and their treatment
items: Stressed assets show up through signs such as bounced cheques, stock shortages and deterioration in asset quality.
Restructured assets are loans that get a longer repayment period at a reduced interest rate.
The SARFAESI Act was framed to help banks recover bad loans and deal better with non-performing assets.
Under Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR), lenders to a corporate borrower can convert the whole or part of their loans into equity shares.
The Reserve Bank of India is the regulator that controls banking and financial services in India.
SIDBI, the small industries bank, has its headquarters at Lucknow.

blocks.title: Minimum CAR
blocks.text: As per the 2024-25 syllabus, scheduled commercial banks in India are required to maintain a minimum CAR of 9%. The figure is a regulatory norm and can be revised by the RBI.
